title: Japan in 12 days
summary: Twelve days by train: Tokyo, a day in Nikko, a night under Mount Fuji, Kyoto and Nara, Osaka, Hiroshima and Miyajima. Probably the best trip of our lives, mostly because of the people.
story: We went for the shrines and temples, Mount Fuji and the food. Japan felt like an intense mix of the future and the past: the neon glow of Akihabara one night, a centuries-old shrine in a cedar forest the next morning. But what we remember most is the people: a cab driver who went out of his way to show us Fuji, a train driver who stepped off his train to help us buy tickets, strangers who stopped whenever we looked lost. Their stories are further down. We came home grateful.
note: Walk times are routing estimates (FOSSGIS foot router) for the stops in order, excluding time spent at them; train times are roughly what our trips took.

takeaways: Nothing gets lost in Japan, so travel light: send your suitcases ahead and carry a backpack.
You don’t need a car. Trains, a highway bus and the odd cab took us everywhere, and we never regretted it.
Ride the Shinkansen at least once; for a long ride, the Green Car is worth it.
Go early, or go where the tripods aren’t. The quiet places felt like heaven.
Leave room for the unplanned: a drinks fair, a food festival, sushi in a castle. They were the best moments.
Covered shopping streets and markets run for blocks, some underground. A rainy day can be spent entirely under them.
Shops and services fill every floor of a building, not just the street level. Look up.

items.point: Two religions, intertwined: Shinto and Buddhism.
items.detail: Shinto is Japan’s own faith, of kami (gods and spirits) in nature, ancestors and places. Buddhism arrived in the 6th century, from India by way of China and Korea. For over a thousand years the two blended: kami were seen as local forms of Buddhas, and shrines and temples often shared grounds. The government formally separated them in 1868, but you still see them side by side, as in Nikko.

items.point: Shrines are Shinto, temples are Buddhist.
items.detail: A shrine has a torii gate: bow twice, clap twice, pray, bow once more. A temple has a sanmon gate: bow and pray with your hands together, no clapping.

items.point: Hindu gods came to Japan with Buddhism.
items.detail: This surprised me most. Buddhism brought many Indian gods with it, renamed and recast as protectors of the Buddha: Bonten is Brahma, Taishakuten is Indra (the two often stand either side of a Buddha; Tōdai-ji has 8th-century statues of the pair), Benzaiten is Saraswati, Daikokuten comes from Mahākāla, a fierce form of Shiva, and Bishamonten or Tamonten is Vaiśravaṇa, the Kubera of Hindu tradition. Kannon, the Bodhisattva of compassion at Sensō-ji and Kiyomizu-dera, is Avalokiteśvara. There is no Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva trinity as such; the triad I saw at Nikko is Buddhist. Nara is where this first caught my attention, and it made me want to learn more.

items.point: Nara, then Kyoto, then Tokyo.
items.detail: Nara was Japan’s first permanent capital, from 710 to 784. After ten years at Nagaoka, the capital moved to Kyoto in 794 and stayed for over a thousand years. Real power often sat elsewhere, with the shoguns in Kamakura and then Edo, today’s Tokyo, which became the capital in 1868. Nikko was never a capital: it is where Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Edo shogunate, is enshrined.

items.point: Our cab driver at Mount Fuji made the trip.
items.detail: Fuji was hidden when we arrived, so we took a cab to Iyashi-no-Sato Nenba, a little sceptical and talking only through a translation app. He worked out that we hadn’t seen Fuji yet, watched for it, and stopped as soon as it appeared. At Nenba he offered to wait, and waited an hour or two without asking for anything. On the way back he asked if we’d like to see a local favourite: he drove up an unpaved road, hard on his car (we briefly wondered if this was a kidnapping), to Kōyōdai, a viewpoint run by an old couple. Best view of Fuji of the trip, and no one else there. Then he took us to Oishi Park.

items.point: Tipping is frowned on, so we asked first.
items.detail: We wanted to thank him properly. We put the money in an envelope and asked, politely, whether he’d mind if we gave him more than the agreed fare. He hesitated, then accepted.

items.point: A train driver got off his train to help us buy tickets.
items.detail: We thought our pass was enough; it wasn’t, and the train was minutes from leaving. The driver stepped down, walked us to the ticket machine, watched us fumble, took over, worked out the fare, waited calmly while we fumbled with the cash, and then got back into his cab.

items.point: In Hiroshima, strangers kept stopping to help.
items.detail: Every time we stood looking lost at a map for a few minutes, someone stopped to guide us. It happened again and again, in the city that has suffered more than any other.

items.point: Pride in the work, even in small things.
items.detail: An old cab driver looked almost hurt when I loaded my own suitcase into his car, and wouldn’t let me hold his bag to make his seat more comfortable. On the Shinkansen, the ticket inspector bowed and treated every passenger with the same quiet respect.

items.point: We didn’t speak Japanese, and it hardly mattered.
items.detail: We should have prepared better, and communication was a struggle. Yet everywhere we went, people found a way to help. We came home grateful to the people we met, and for being lucky enough to see Japan this way.

items.point: We felt completely safe, at any hour.
items.detail: We walked around late at night without a worry. Bright streets and shops open late made the cities feel alive rather than empty.

items.point: Public transport everywhere, and no regrets.
items.detail: Unlike our Central Europe trip, we didn’t rent a car. Trains took us everywhere, plus one highway bus to Mount Fuji, a boat to Miyajima, and the odd cab.

items.point: Take the Shinkansen, and treat yourself to the Green Car.
items.detail: We took three bullet trains: from near Mount Fuji to Kyoto, Osaka to Hiroshima, and Hiroshima back to Tokyo. Smooth, comfortable and fast; we loved every ride. For the long one back to Tokyo we upgraded to the Green Car (first class), and the service was excellent. Pick up a bento at the station before you board.

items.point: Send your luggage ahead, and skip a stop.
items.detail: Most hotels will forward your suitcase to your next hotel for a small fee, with handwritten forms and no computer system in sight. It always arrived on time. Our trick: send it two stops ahead (Tokyo straight to Kyoto, say) and carry a backpack for the night in between. When ours hadn’t reached Kyoto yet, the hotel staff said, “Nothing gets lost in Japan.” They were right.

items.point: Get a Suica or Pasmo card.
items.detail: One card works on most city trains and metros, and in convenience stores. The Shinkansen (bullet train) is ticketed separately. Check whether your pass covers each train before you board.

items.point: Your phone does the rest.
items.detail: An eSIM before you land, Google Maps for train routes and platforms, and a camera translation app (Google Translate, Papago) for menus and signs.

items.point: The best meal: teppanyaki in Hiroshima.
items.detail: Wagyu, seafood and vegetables cooked on the grill in front of us.

items.point: The best bite: black beef sushi inside Osaka Castle.
items.detail: It was raining, so we ducked into the shops in the castle grounds. Who expects great food there? It was the best single bite of the trip.

items.point: Some of the best food was unplanned.
items.detail: A Japanese drinks fair we stumbled into in Akihabara (buy coupons, taste everything), a food festival in Nara Park, grilled oysters on Miyajima, a fried-dumpling place with endless dumplings and cold Japanese beer, matcha beer in Tokyo, and a bottle of plain milk at the milk stand in Akihabara Station that we still talk about.

items.point: Go to a convenience store every day.
items.detail: We did, for random desserts, fried chicken that was always juicy, and fruit sandos: soft white bread with cream and fresh fruit, the best of all, and often sold out. One day we went to Be! Fruits Sandwich at Tokyo Station, which sells nothing but fruit sandos. 7-Eleven for onigiri and sandwiches, FamilyMart for fried chicken, Lawson for desserts. With a store open on almost every corner, we never worried about food or drinks.

items.point: Look out for the fresh orange juice machines.
items.detail: Cheap machines that squeeze oranges on the spot, in several places. After a long day walking in the heat and humidity, they were a lifesaver.

items.point: Meals there are long and slow.
items.detail: At izakaya-style places we would order a few dishes, eat, drink, order more, and keep going for three or four hours. It’s a different rhythm from the one-main-course dinners we’re used to elsewhere, and we loved it.

items.point: The beer tasted different, and we can’t explain why.
items.detail: Nothing fancy, just the everyday Asahi and the rest. They all say “dry” on the label, but they didn’t taste dry, and the same labels at home don’t taste the same. Our best guess is freshness: in Japan it’s brewed nearby and served fresh and very cold, often on draft, while abroad it has travelled for weeks or is brewed under licence elsewhere. We could have drunk a lot of it.

items.point: Markets, and miles of covered streets.
items.detail: Tsukiji, Nishiki, and the long covered shopping streets were highlights in themselves: you can walk for blocks under cover, or underground. Try Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki in Hiroshima.

items.point: Kyoto was crowded, but it is truly the cultural capital.
items.detail: The famous spots were packed with people chasing the perfect photo, which took some of the joy out of them. Even so, nowhere else felt so full of history and culture. Go early, or pick the quieter temples.

items.point: Go early, and look for the quiet places.
items.detail: The famous spots are crowded, and full of photographers with tripods. Early mornings, and places like Kōyōdai where we were alone, felt like the real Japan.

items.point: The days are short in early autumn.
items.detail: It gets dark around 5 pm, and most sights close about then. Plan the important ones for the morning.

items.point: Bring comfortable shoes.
items.detail: We walked so much that our feet hurt.

items.point: Dōtonbori was a disappointment.
items.detail: The food was so-so, and it was the least clean place we saw in Japan; we even saw rats near the restaurants.

items.point: Akihabara after midnight shows another side.
items.detail: Our first night, we walked out after midnight and found women in anime costumes handing out flyers for “girlfriend” bars, where men pay for company and conversation. Harmless, but it felt strange next to everything else we saw.
